Most models treated the head's "is disabled" flag as SNAP elderly/disabled-household status. That status would remove the shelter cap and allow the excess medical deduction, so their net income came out near zero and their benefit near the maximum. SNAP defines a disabled member by receipt of a disability-based benefit such as SSI or SSDI (7 U.S.C. 2012(j)), and this head receives none. SSI is $0 because countable earned and unearned income exceed the federal benefit rate. The household still qualifies through California's broad-based categorical eligibility (TANF non-cash), with gross income of $2,120 against a 200% FPL limit. Net income is then $2,120.25 minus the $290.72 earned-income deduction, the $209 standard deduction and the $744 capped shelter deduction, or $876.51. That gives $298 − $262.80 = $35.20 a month for January to September and $48.18 a month for October to December after the FY2027 uprating, $461.34 for the year. The models that answered $0 made the opposite mistake: they applied the 130% gross income test or misjudged the limits and missed the categorical-eligibility pathway. Developer adjudication (2026-09-05): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated prompt_ambiguity (age_disability). The output is removed from scoring for every model: its reference depends on an engine input the certified household data never carried and the prompt therefore never listed, and a careful reader could take the stated facts the other way. Recomputed with policyengine-us 1.755.4 (the version that produced the references) the reference moves from 461.339722 to 3596.039795 under the alternative reading. Neither reading is established by the facts; rows that matched the frozen value leave the score along with rows that did not. Judge diagnoses are retained as description; the class prompt_ambiguity records that the reference, not the model, is indeterminate here. SSI itself stays $0 under either reading (the head's countable income exceeds the federal benefit rate); SNAP moves because SSI-disabled status switches on the elderly-or-disabled SNAP rules.

SSI requires the individual to satisfy the aged, blind, or disabled categorical gate before income exclusions or benefit-rate calculations apply. The head's unlisted SSI disability status is false under the prompt instructions, so `is_ssi_aged_blind_disabled=False` and SSI is $0 without an income calculation.

Taxable income is $16,828.34: CA AGI of $22,534.34 (wages less the 401(k) deferral and IRA deduction, plus the $8,000 403(b) distribution) minus the $5,706 standard deduction. At 2025 brackets (1% to $11,079, then 2%) that yields $225.78, which is only slightly more than the $213 of nonrefundable credits ($153 personal exemption credit plus $60 renter's credit), so $12.78 remains. The wrong answers fall into four groups. Many models said the credits wipe out the tax without doing the subtraction. Others dropped the $8,000 403(b) distribution or one of the two credits. The rest used 2026 deduction and credit values they projected themselves or stale 2023/2024 values, when PolicyEngine holds the published 2025 amounts. Because the true remainder is so small, errors of a few dollars in any input swing the answer between $0 and about $20.

This childless 28-year-old California filer qualifies for the CalEITC. CalEITC is a standalone state credit: it does not depend on the federal EITC, and its childless phase-out runs to roughly $32,000, well above the federal childless ceiling. The credit uses both earned income ($17,442.65) and AGI ($22,534.34). The $8,000 taxable 403(b) distribution pushes AGI above earnings, so AGI sets the credit and leaves only $95.15 near the bottom of the phase-out. The models that answered $0 either used the federal childless income ceiling, tied CalEITC to federal EITC, treated the 403(b) distribution as disqualifying investment income, or denied childless eligibility or refundability. Most of the models that answered too high phased the credit out on earned income alone, ignored the phase-out, or used inaccurate 2026 phase-out parameters.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The case turns entirely on the 2026 parameter set: OBBBA made the TCJA structure permanent and inflation-indexed, so the MFJ standard deduction is $32,200, there are no personal exemptions, and the brackets are 10% to $24,800 then 12%. AGI is uncontested at $94,925.30 ($62,725.29 employment income + $32,200 taxable pension), itemizing yields only $2,354.43, and no nonrefundable credit applies to a childless couple with no care or education expenses, so taxable income is $62,725.30 and tax is $2,480 + 0.12 × $37,925.30 = $7,031.04. The wrong answers split into three families: models that applied a TCJA-sunset baseline (~$16,600 deduction plus ~$10,600 of exemptions and a 15% second bracket, landing near $8,900–$9,150), models that anchored on 2025 or invented deduction/bracket figures ($29,900–$31,450 deductions, $23,850–$24,600 bracket tops, landing $7,130–$7,314), and models that derived the right number or a near-right number and then submitted a different one.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.
Medicare eligibility requires age 65 in the absence of a qualifying disability, ESRD, or other explicitly listed pathway. The 61-year-old head has no such condition, so the age test yields 0 (No).

The employee-side payroll tax base here is exactly one number: the spouse's $62,725 of gross wages. The head reports no wages at all (only ESI premiums, hours, and medical expenses), the spouse's $32,200 taxable private pension is not FICA wages, employer-sponsored insurance premiums are not netted out of the FICA base in PolicyEngine's employee_payroll_tax, and Ohio imposes no mandatory employee-side state payroll tax (no employee SDI/UI, and state income tax is a separate output). So the answer is 6.2% + 1.45% on $62,725 = $3,888.97 Social Security + $909.52 Medicare = $4,798.48, with no Additional Medicare Tax below the $250,000 MFJ threshold. Every wrong answer either enlarged or shrank that $62,725 base, bolted on a nonexistent state levy or the employer share, or submitted a number that contradicted its own correct arithmetic.

The correct calculation starts from Ohio AGI of $94,925 (spouse wages plus the taxable private pension). It subtracts two $1,900 personal exemptions, which is the tier for Ohio AGI above $80,000, leaving taxable income of $91,125. Ohio's 2026 schedule then gives a $332 base tax plus 2.75% on income above $26,050, which is $2,121.57, and the $200 retirement income credit (for $8,000 or more of retirement income) brings it to $1,921.57. The main trap is that $332 base tax. Six models got every other step right, dropped the base, and landed at $1,589.56, exactly $332 low. Most of the other models also made one or more of these errors: they used the wrong exemption tier ($2,150, $2,400 and so on), left out the $200 retirement credit, used the stale $360.69 base from 2024, or subtracted deductions Ohio does not allow, such as the federal standard deduction or employer insurance premiums.

CHIP eligibility requires the child to be ineligible for Medicaid; it is not determined merely by comparing household income with the CHIP ceiling. Child 1 qualifies for Medicaid under North Carolina's OLDER_CHILD category, so the Medicaid determination precludes CHIP eligibility.

North Carolina covers children aged 6 to 18 in Medicaid's older-child category up to 211% FPL, plus the 5-point MAGI disregard, because NC Health Choice was folded into Medicaid. The household's MAGI is the spouse's $85,209 in wages (overtime is already included) minus the $2,778 traditional 401(k) and $130 traditional IRA contributions, which gives $82,301. That is 2.13 times the 2026 poverty line for a family of five, so it falls inside the limit. Most models used the old 133%/138% federal minimum for school-age children. Others added the overtime a second time, skipped the pre-tax deductions, used an old poverty line, or treated employer-sponsored insurance as disqualifying. Medicaid has no uninsured requirement, so that insurance does not matter here.

CHIP eligibility requires the child not to qualify for Medicaid; it is not established solely by comparing household MAGI with a CHIP income ceiling. Child 2 qualifies for Medicaid under the OLDER_CHILD category, so Medicaid precedence excludes the child from CHIP regardless of the CHIP income threshold.

North Carolina moved its separate NC Health Choice CHIP program into Medicaid in April 2023. Children aged 6-18 therefore sit in the Medicaid OLDER_CHILD category up to 211% FPL, or 216% with the 5-point MAGI disregard, instead of the old 133%/138% Medicaid tier. The household's MAGI is the spouse's wages less traditional 401(k) and IRA contributions, about $82,300, which is 2.13 times the 2026 FPL for five people. That puts child2 inside the limit. Most models used the obsolete 133% limit and sent the child to a separate CHIP. The rest either applied 211% without the disregard, understated the 2026 five-person FPL, which pushed the ratio above the limit, or wrongly treated employer-sponsored insurance as a bar to Medicaid.

CHIP eligibility requires the child to be ineligible for Medicaid, so satisfying a CHIP age or income condition is not sufficient. Child 3 qualifies for Medicaid under North Carolina's OLDER_CHILD category, and that Medicaid eligibility makes the child ineligible for CHIP regardless of the cited CHIP income thresholds.

North Carolina folded its NC Health Choice CHIP band into Medicaid in 2023. Since then, its Medicaid older-child category (ages 6-18) has covered children up to 211% FPL, which the 5-point MAGI disregard raises to about 216%. The household's MAGI is about $82,301: the $85,209 in wages minus $2,778 in traditional 401(k) and $130 in traditional IRA contributions. That is 2.13 times the 2026 FPL for a family of five, so child3 falls inside the Medicaid older-child limit. Most models used the old 133%/138% FPL limit for children aged 6-18 and pushed the 138-211% band into CHIP. Others used a limit near 211% but measured gross wages, used a stale or wrong FPL, dropped the 5% disregard, or wrongly treated employer coverage as a bar to Medicaid.

2026 law keeps the TCJA structure — personal exemptions repealed, a $32,200 MFJ standard deduction — and adds the deduction for qualified FLSA overtime premiums, so the $7,746.26 premium comes out of taxable income rather than being stacked onto wages that already include it, leaving $42,354.26 taxable and $4,586.51 of tentative tax. The child tax credit is $2,200 per qualifying child in 2026, and its nonrefundable portion offsets the entire liability first, with the $1,700-per-child ACTC as the residual, so $6,600 of credit for three children drives the answer to exactly $0. The wrong answers split into two clusters: models that applied the expired pre-TCJA regime (a reverted ~$16,600 standard deduction, ~$5,200 personal exemptions, a 15% bracket, a $1,000-per-child credit), and models that got the deduction stack roughly right but capped the nonrefundable CTC at $500–$1,100 per child by treating the refundable ACTC as consumed first. Every wrong model ignored the qualified-overtime deduction, and three double-counted the $7,746 premium on top of the $85,209 gross wage figure.

This is 2026 law under OBBBA. The CTC is $2,200 per child, so $6,600 for three children, and the refundable portion is capped at $1,700 per child. The spouse's $7,746 FLSA overtime premium is deductible as qualified overtime compensation. AGI is $82,301 ($85,209 minus $2,778 traditional 401k and $130 IRA). Subtracting the $32,200 standard deduction and the $7,746 overtime deduction leaves taxable income of about $42,355, which gives pre-credit tax of about $4,586.51. That tax absorbs only $4,586.51 of the $6,600 CTC. The remaining $2,013.49 is refundable because it is below both the $5,100 cap and the limit of 15% of earnings over $2,500. Most models got this wrong in one of four ways: they used the pre-OBBBA $2,000 credit or the TCJA-sunset $1,000 credit, they left out the overtime deduction and so treated tax as large enough to absorb the whole credit, they deducted the wrong items, or they treated the refundable amount as a fixed per-child figure.

Free school meals require income within the free-meal limit or categorical eligibility through a qualifying program. This household's countable income of $85,208.82 equals 220% of the $38,680 federal poverty guideline, exceeds even the 185% reduced-price limit, and has no categorical eligibility, so its school-meal tier is paid.

The entire liability is 6.2% plus 1.45% on the Spouse's $85,209 of gross wages: $5,282.95 + $1,235.53 = $6,518.47, with no Additional Medicare Tax below the $250,000 MFJ threshold and no mandatory North Carolina employee payroll tax. The trap is the base: the separately listed $7,746 FSLA overtime premium is a decomposition of those same wages, not extra earnings, and the $21,208 employer-sponsored insurance premium sits on the Head, who has zero wages, while employee FICA is levied on gross employment income with no Section 125 exclusion. Five models moved the base — inflating it with the overtime premium, shrinking it by the ESI premium, or both — one invented a state payroll tax, one included the employer Social Security share, one zeroed the base outright, and one lost the value to a $1.48 arithmetic slip.

Reduced-price school meals require household income at or below 185% of the federal poverty guideline or a qualifying categorical-eligibility pathway. The household's school-meal income is $85,209, equal to 2.20 times the guideline, and it has neither universal-free-meal coverage nor categorical eligibility, so its tier is PAID.

Connecticut uses broad-based categorical eligibility (BBCE). The household's $2,536.25 monthly gross income is under 200% FPL, so it is categorically eligible and skips both the resource test and the 100% FPL net income test. Because an eligible one- or two-person household gets the minimum allotment even when the benefit formula gives zero, it receives $24 a month, or $288 a year. The formula gives zero here because the $636 expected contribution is more than the $546 maximum allotment. Blindness or disability alone does not establish Medicaid eligibility; the spouse qualifies through none of Connecticut's modeled categorical pathways, so the Medicaid category is NONE. Her Medicaid MAGI is 1.41 times FPL, above the applicable MAGI-category limit, and she receives no SSI to establish an SSI-linked pathway.

Medicare eligibility attaches to the individual, and PolicyEngine's is_medicare_eligible turns on that person's own age being 65 or older — the head at 68 returns True, the spouse at 39 returns False, and an `is_disabled` or `is_blind` flag opens no separate route in the engine. The statutory under-65 pathway (42 U.S.C. §426(b)) requires 24 months of the person's own entitlement to Social Security disability insurance benefits, which requires insured status from that person's own work credits; the spouse here has $0 of disability income and $0 of earnings under the "treat any unlisted numeric input as 0" instruction, so the $30,160 SSDI belongs solely to the 68-year-old head. Nine models converted the bare "is disabled" demographic flag into an assumed 24-month SSDI entitlement for the spouse, and one invented a derivative pathway in which a Social Security beneficiary's disabled spouse gets Medicare — no such pathway exists. Being disabled is not the same as being entitled to disability benefits, and Medicare entitlement never passes from one spouse to another.

Most wrong answers correctly identified this base and these rates but then replaced their own exact result with an unsupported rounded or adjusted number.

Self-employment tax is a nonnegative liability assessed only on positive net earnings from self-employment. The listed negative SSTB amount does not create a negative self-employment tax or refundable tax offset, so the self-employment tax base and liability are both zero.

The case turns on one parameter set: for tax year 2026 a single filer's standard deduction is $16,100 with no personal exemption, and the rate schedule is 10% to $12,400 then 12% to $50,400, so $59,220 of taxable pension income leaves $43,120 taxable and $1,240 + 12% x $30,720 = $4,926.40, with no nonrefundable credits available to a 56-year-old with no dependents. Eight models assumed the TCJA individual provisions lapse and rebuilt the return on a pre-TCJA base of roughly an $8,300 standard deduction plus a $5,300 personal exemption and a 15% second bracket, landing near $6,250; another cluster carried stale 2023-2025 deductions and bracket edges into 2026 and landed near $5,070-$5,120. A third cluster reached $4,926 exactly and then overrode it with an unexplained figure. Secondary traps — inferring mortgage interest from a loan balance, itemizing medical costs below the 7.5% AGI floor, head-of-household filing, and an elderly credit that requires age 65 — account for the remaining misses.

New Jersey Medicaid requires both membership in a qualifying eligibility category and satisfaction of that category's financial rules. This 56-year-old has medicaid_category NONE, and MAGI income of 3.71 times FPL exceeds the limits for all applicable MAGI pathways; the listed expenses and assets do not create another pathway.

Taxable private pension income is not wages and is excluded from the employee Social Security, Medicare, and mandatory state payroll-tax bases. With no wages or other earned income listed, every employee-side payroll-tax component is zero.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

A 56-year-old who is not disabled cannot use New Jersey's pension exclusion, which requires age 62 or disability, so the whole $59,220 pension counts as NJ gross income. The only reduction is the $1,000 single personal exemption, which leaves $58,220 of taxable income. The schedule then gives 1.4%×20,000 + 1.75%×15,000 + 3.5%×5,000 + 5.525%×18,220 = $1,724.16. No NJ medical expense deduction applies, because qualifying costs are $1,000 of non-employer premiums plus $100 of other medical expenses, or $1,100, which is below the 2%-of-gross-income floor of $1,184.40. Employer-sponsored premiums are pre-tax coverage, the 'excluding Medicare Part B' premium line is the same $1,000 as the other-premiums line, and over-the-counter costs are not deductible. The models went wrong in two main ways: seven granted the age-restricted pension exclusion, and eleven built a medical deduction by stacking ESI premiums, double-counting the $1,000 premium, or adding OTC costs.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The case turns on one 2026 provision: the OBBBA below-the-line deduction for qualified FLSA overtime premium, which lets a non-itemizer stack $9,629.03 on top of the $16,100 single standard deduction, cutting taxable income from $25,439 to $15,810.43 and tax from $2,804.68 to $1,649.25 under the 2026 schedule (10% to $12,400, then 12%). A second trap is the $5,789 employer-sponsored insurance premium, which does not reduce the stated $41,943.38 of employment income — only the $385.90 traditional 401(k) deferral and the $18.03 traditional IRA deduction do. A third cluster assumed TCJA sunset parameters (an ~$8,300 standard deduction, a ~$5,300 personal exemption and a 15% second bracket), all of which OBBBA superseded, and a fourth applied a saver's credit whose rate is 0% at AGI $41,539. Every wrong answer traces to one or more of these four.

A 44-year-old single filer with no dependent children or qualifying education expenses and $41,943 of wages receives neither EITC nor refundable CTC. All other refundable federal credit components evaluated to zero, so federal refundable credits total $0.

North Carolina’s Medicaid expansion does not make every adult aged 19–64 eligible; the expansion pathway applies an income limit. At 2.60 times FPL, the head exceeds the applicable MAGI threshold and qualifies through no other Medicaid category, so the eligibility category is NONE.

Employee-side payroll tax here is a flat application of 6.2% OASDI and 1.45% HI to the full $41,943 of gross wages: $2,600.49 + $608.18 = $3,208.67, with no wage-base cap in play, no Additional Medicare Tax, and no mandatory employee payroll tax in North Carolina. The trap is the payroll-tax base: the listed $5,789 employer-sponsored insurance premium is an employer-paid premium input, not a section 125 salary-reduction election, so it does not shrink FICA wages; likewise the $404 of traditional 401(k)/IRA contributions and the $9,629 FLSA overtime premium leave the FICA base untouched (the overtime deduction is income-tax-only). Seven models subtracted the $5,789 premium and landed on 7.65% × $36,154 = $2,765.78, understating the tax by ~$443. The remaining wrong models identified the correct base and rates but submitted figures inconsistent with their own arithmetic, or submitted nothing.

North Carolina's 2026 individual income tax is a single flat 3.99% rate on federal AGI less the $12,750 single standard deduction, so the whole case turns on building the right base: AGI = $41,943 wages less only the traditional 401(k) ($386) and deductible traditional IRA ($18), i.e. $41,539.45, giving $28,789.45 taxable and $1,148.70 of tax. Two subtractions are traps: the $5,789 employer-sponsored insurance premium is already excluded from the reported wage figure and is not a further above-the-line adjustment, and the $9,629 FLSA overtime premium feeds a below-the-line federal deduction that never touches AGI and that North Carolina does not conform to. Nine models subtracted the ESI premium (AGI $35,750 → $23,000 taxable → $917.70), three subtracted the overtime premium (AGI $31,910 → $19,160 taxable → ~$764), and most of the remainder substituted a stale rate (4.75%, 4.5%, 4.25%, 4.0%) or an invented standard deduction ($10,750, $13,750, $15,400, $15,500, $21,500) for the 2026 parameters. Several models reached $1,148.68 in their own work and then submitted a different number.

CHIP is residual coverage: it reaches only children who fail Medicaid, so a CHIP determination requires a Medicaid floor test before any CHIP ceiling test. Household income of ~$22,992 for a family of four is roughly 71% FPL, far under Louisiana's Medicaid limit for children ages 6–18 (142% FPL), so 7-year-old child1 is Medicaid-eligible under the OLDER_CHILD category and CHIP eligibility is therefore 0. Every wrong model screened only against an upper LaCHIP ceiling (200–250% FPL), read "income well below the ceiling" as qualifying, and never applied the lower bound — the very fact that made the answer No.

Head Start for preschool-age children requires the child to fall within the program’s preschool age range; a seven-year-old does not satisfy that categorical requirement. Income eligibility cannot override the age restriction, so Child 1 is ineligible even under an income calculation that falls below a poverty guideline.

Louisiana evaluates a 7-year-old under the Medicaid older-child category. The household's MAGI is 0.66 times FPL, below that category's 2026 income limit, so the child qualifies; the listed assets do not alter this MAGI eligibility determination.
WIC child eligibility is limited to children under age five. Child 1 is age seven, so the child fails the categorical age requirement regardless of household income.

CHIP is residual to Medicaid: a child who qualifies for Medicaid cannot be CHIP-eligible, so the operative test for a 6-year-old is the Medicaid children's MAGI screen, not the CHIP ceiling. Household MAGI of roughly $22,993 for a family of four sits near 71% of FPL, far under the OLDER_CHILD (ages 6–18) Medicaid limit, so child2 is Medicaid-eligible and therefore excluded from CHIP. Every wrong model ran a single test — income versus a 202–250% FPL CHIP ceiling — found the household comfortably under it, and answered "eligible," never screening the child against Medicaid first. Being far below the CHIP limit is exactly what makes the child Medicaid-eligible and thus CHIP-ineligible; the models read the same fact in the opposite direction.

Head Start preschool eligibility requires satisfying the program’s applicable age and income rules; a six-year-old is outside the ordinary preschool-age category, and no fact establishes an exception such as delayed kindergarten entry. The household contains four people, and PolicyEngine’s traced income test also does not place this child within the qualifying threshold, so low income alone cannot produce eligibility.

Louisiana evaluates the 6-year-old under the older-child Medicaid category using household MAGI relative to the applicable child income limit. The household's MAGI is 0.66 times FPL, so the child satisfies that category's income test; the listed assets do not disqualify a MAGI-category child.

WIC child eligibility ends at the child’s fifth birthday, so a six-year-old is categorically ineligible regardless of household income. All four models incorrectly treated age six as falling within the WIC child category; the models that also evaluated income therefore never reached the correct result because they first misapplied the age rule.

The requested amount cannot fall below zero: taxable income and income tax before credits are zero, and nonrefundable credits used are capped at the existing tax liability. Refundable credits are excluded from this output, so the resulting federal income tax before refundable credits is $0.

Earned income is wages ($7,468) plus SE income minus the deductible half of SE tax, about $21,896. That puts this married-filing-jointly two-child family on the 2026 EITC plateau at the $7,316 maximum. The refundable CTC is 15% x (earned income - $2,500) = $2,909.35. It stays below the $1,700-per-child refundable cap, which OBBBA's permanent $2,200 CTC keeps in place for 2026. Most models went wrong in one of four ways: they assumed the TCJA CTC expired and reverted to $1,000/child with a $3,000 threshold; they guessed the wrong EITC maximum; they paid the flat $1,700 or $1,800/child cap and skipped the 15% earned-income limit; or they measured SE earnings wrongly (gross, 92.35%, or reduced twice) in the ACTC base.

The household qualifies for the free tier through two independent routes: SNAP receipt confers categorical eligibility, and school-meal income is 70% of the federal poverty guideline, below the 130% cutoff. The two K–12 children therefore generate positive annual free-school-meal support, so the binary output is Yes.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The trap is Louisiana's ACA adult expansion: LA adopted expansion effective July 1, 2016, so a 25-year-old non-disabled, non-pregnant adult qualifies through the MAGI ADULT category at up to 138% FPL, with no resource test. The household's countable MAGI of about $22,992 (wages $7,468 plus self-employment $15,525) measured against the four-person poverty line is 0.66 FPL — less than half the 138% ceiling — so the head clears the only test that applies. Every wrong model priced the head against a pre-expansion parent/caretaker standard (or an asset screen) instead of running the single MAGI-versus-138%-FPL comparison, and none of them actually computed the FPL ratio the record supplies.

WIC does not extend categorical eligibility to a parent or caretaker merely because children live in the household. The head is not specified as pregnant, postpartum, or breastfeeding, and the children are ages 7 and 6, above WIC's under-5 age limit, so income eligibility and adjunctive eligibility cannot make the head eligible.

The requested payroll-tax output includes only employee-side FICA on the head’s wage earnings; self-employment income belongs in the separate self-employment-tax output. PolicyEngine applies the underlying wage amount and component-level calculations to produce $462.98 of Social Security tax plus $108.28 of Medicare tax, totaling $571.26.

Reduced-price eligibility is a mutually exclusive lower tier, not a general test of whether income is below 185% of the federal poverty guideline. At 70% of the guideline, and with categorical eligibility, this household receives the superior free-meals tier, so reduced-price support is zero.

The SECA computation here is a single closed-form line with no branch points: net earnings from self-employment are $15,525 × 0.9235 = $14,337.3375, and because $7,468 of wages plus that base sit far below the Social Security wage base, the full 15.3% applies, giving exactly $2,193.61. The separating step is executing that arithmetic to the cent and stopping there — the 92.35% factor already embodies the employer-share equivalent, and the one-half-of-SE-tax deduction under §164(f) reduces AGI for income tax only, never the SECA base itself. Seven of the eight wrong answers name the right formula and then miss on execution: rounded or miscomputed multiplications ($2,191.73, $2,192, $2,194.96, $2,196.28, $2,197, $1,360.68) or a second, invalid reduction of the base by the half-SE-tax deduction ($2,054.08).

This SNAP calculation is simple: $1,916.04 of monthly earned income, minus the 20% earned income deduction ($383.21) and the FY2026 four-person standard deduction of $223, gives net income of $1,310. The household has no shelter, dependent care or allowable medical deduction, since no one is elderly or disabled and no rent, mortgage payment or utilities are listed. The benefit is the FY2026 $994 maximum allotment minus $393, which is $601 a month or $7,212 a year. Most models set up the formula correctly but used outdated or guessed parameters: FY2025's $975 maximum and $204 standard deduction, or projected maximums of $1,000 to $1,050. Others invented shelter, dependent or self-employment-cost deductions, or wrongly found the household ineligible.

CHIP eligibility requires the person to be ineligible for Medicaid, not merely under age 19 and below the CHIP income ceiling. The spouse qualifies for Medicaid under Louisiana's OLDER_CHILD category, so Medicaid eligibility precludes CHIP eligibility without regard to whether other coverage was listed.

The trap is that the 18-year-old is labeled \"spouse,\" and all three models let that label override the age-based pathway: PolicyEngine assigns her the OLDER_CHILD medicaid_category, which covers ages 6-18 in Louisiana and does not require being a tax dependent or an unmarried child. The income test is not close either — household MAGI is 0.66 x FPL, below Louisiana's ~142% FPL older-child limit and below the 138% FPL adult expansion limit, so both the child pathway and the adult pathway the models invoked return eligible. Every wrong answer therefore combines a category error (adult instead of older child) with an unperformed or inverted FPL comparison, and one model additionally imported a nonexistent asset test into a MAGI category.

WIC income eligibility does not independently confer eligibility: a person must also be pregnant, breastfeeding, postpartum, an infant, or a child under age five. The spouse is 18, all unlisted statuses are false, and the only children are ages six and seven, so neither parenthood, childbearing age, nor low household income places the spouse in a WIC categorical group.

Louisiana's 2024 tax reform took effect in 2025. It replaced the graduated brackets and the old combined personal exemption–standard deduction ($9,000 MFJ, plus $1,000 per dependent) with a flat 3% rate and a $25,000 standard deduction for joint filers. Federal AGI is $21,896: $22,993 of wages and SE income minus the half-SE-tax deduction of about $1,097. That is below the $25,000 MFJ deduction, so Louisiana taxable income is zero and so is the tax. Most models used pre-reform exemptions and brackets (1.85%, 2%/4%) or applied only the $12,500 single-filer deduction to a joint return, which left positive taxable income. One model reached $0 in its reasoning but submitted a different number.

Louisiana's only applicable refundable credit is the LA EITC, which is refundable and equals 5% of the federal EITC. This joint-filing couple with two children has EITC earned income of about $21,900 (wages plus net self-employment earnings less half of SE tax). That puts them on the plateau, so their federal EITC is the 2026 two-child maximum of $7,316, and the LA credit is 5% × $7,316 = $365.80. Most wrong models split two ways. About half denied that Louisiana has a refundable EITC and answered $0. Most of the rest used the correct 5% rate on a federal EITC that was too high or too low, or used the old 3.5% rate.

reference_bug_hypothesis: PolicyEngine's IRS gross-income sources leave out estate_income, so $25,950 of estate/trust income never enters AGI or the Social Security provisional-income test. That conflicts with IRC §61(a)(15) and §662(a). Its §199A QBI definition still counts the same income, which yields a positive $3,319.81 QBI deduction when the only other business item is a $6,260 loss.
case_annotation: PolicyEngine builds AGI of $32,699.07 without the $25,950 estate income. That puts provisional income at $40,622.47, so only $10,129.10 of Social Security is taxable under the single $25k/$34k thresholds. It then subtracts the $16,100 single standard deduction and a $3,319.81 QBI deduction capped at 20% of $16,599.07, which leaves taxable income of $13,279.25 and tax of $1,345.51. Every model that counted estate income made 85% of benefits taxable and reached about $79,209 of AGI. The largest cluster also used qualifying-surviving-spouse joint brackets and the $32,200 deduction, even though that status needs a dependent child. Others used stale 2025 or TCJA-sunset parameters, or invented credits and deductions. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned reference_engine_defect; adjudicated reference_engine_defect (taxable_income_or_deductions). The frozen reference is 1,345.51; the corrected value is 8,596.03. PolicyEngine leaves estate income out of gross income while counting it as qualified business income. Reference is an engine defect; output excluded from scoring (26 U.S.C. 61(a)(14), 662(a), 199A(c)(3)(A)(ii)).
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Every Virginia Medicaid pathway open to a 61-year-old is income-tested: the ACA expansion adult group caps MAGI at 138% FPL, and the SSI-linked aged/blind/disabled group sits far below that and keys off SSI receipt, which is $0 here. This head's Medicaid MAGI counts the full $36,105 Social Security benefit (untaxed portion included) plus $26,800 in IRA distributions, $2,030 in pension, and $25,950 in estate income, offset only by a $6,260 self-employment loss, landing at 368% FPL — 2.7x the expansion limit — so the engine assigns medicaid_category NONE. All three models either asserted without arithmetic that MAGI fell under 138% FPL or treated the "is disabled" flag as a categorical pass that skips the income test entirely. Disability and the expansion group's waived asset test change which income test applies, never whether one applies.

The head is 61, so the only route to Medicare is the under-65 pathway. That pathway requires 24 months of entitlement to Social Security disability benefits, or end-stage renal disease. Being flagged "disabled" does not meet it. The household lists no SSDI receipt and no ESRD. Its only Social Security income is retirement income, and unlisted inputs such as months of disability benefits count as 0. So the head is not Medicare eligible. Every wrong model treated the general disability flag, sometimes together with the Social Security retirement income, as enough for Medicare.

Employee payroll tax applies to wage and salary income, not estate income, Social Security retirement benefits, IRA distributions, private pensions, or self-employment income. No wages were listed, and the prompt requires unlisted numeric inputs to be zero, so the employee Social Security, Medicare, Additional Medicare, and mandatory state payroll-tax bases are all zero.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

reference_bug_hypothesis: PolicyEngine leaves the head's $25,950 estate income out of federal gross income and AGI. The trace AGI of $32,699.07 equals IRA $26,800 + pension $2,030 - SE loss $6,260 + taxable Social Security $10,129.10, which contradicts IRC §61(a)(15) and §662(a): both put estate distributions in the beneficiary's gross income. With that income included, Virginia AGI is $48,520, taxable income is $38,840, and the tax is $1,975.80.
case_annotation: The reference's federal AGI of $32,699.07 is built from IRA ($26,800), pension ($2,030), the -$6,260 self-employment loss and $10,129.10 of taxable Social Security under single-filer thresholds. It contains no estate income. After the Social Security subtraction, Virginia AGI is $22,569.97. The $8,750 standard deduction and $930 exemption then leave $12,889.97 of taxable income, taxed at $60 + $60 + $394.50 = $514.50. Nearly every model added the $25,950 estate income to AGI, which gives Virginia AGI of $48,520 and a tax of $1,969-$2,029 (exactly $1,975.80 with the $8,750 deduction and $930 exemption). A second group also treated the head as a qualifying surviving spouse and took the $17,500 joint deduction, although with no dependent child the head files single. Others skipped the full taxable Social Security subtraction or invented age or disability exclusions that do not apply to a 61-year-old whose income is pension, IRA and estate income. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned reference_engine_defect; adjudicated reference_engine_defect (taxable_income_or_deductions). The frozen reference is 514.50; the corrected value is 1,975.80. PolicyEngine leaves estate income out of gross income while counting it as qualified business income. Reference is an engine defect; output excluded from scoring (26 U.S.C. 61(a)(14), 662(a), 199A(c)(3)(A)(ii)).
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Every model got the same AGI the engine used ($28,000 wages + $4,300 taxable Social Security = $32,300, since workers' compensation is excluded and provisional income of $40,600 falls in the 50% tier between the $32,000 and $44,000 MFJ thresholds) or missed it, and then lost the case on the deduction side. For tax year 2026 the TCJA structure is permanent: personal exemptions remain repealed, the MFJ standard deduction is $32,200, the aged additional standard deduction is $1,650 per 65+ spouse ($3,300), and the OBBBA senior deduction adds $6,000 per spouse aged 65+ ($12,000) for a total of $47,500 — well above the $32,300 AGI, so taxable income and tax are $0. Six of the nine models instead applied a TCJA-sunset 2026 with a ~$16,500–$20,000 standard deduction plus revived personal exemptions of ~$10,200–$10,600, a combination that leaves a small positive taxable income taxed at 10%. The two that used a post-OBBBA standard deduction still failed by inflating includible Social Security or by treating the senior deduction as a tax offset rather than a $6,000-per-spouse deduction.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Arizona Medicaid expansion does not cover the head through the ordinary adult MAGI pathway because the head is over 65, and the head qualifies through none of the aged, blind, or disabled pathways. At 2.46 times FPL, with no SSI, no disability, and no dependent status, the head has Medicaid category NONE and is ineligible.

Employee payroll tax applies separately to both spouses' wages and equals $1,736 of Social Security tax plus $406 of Medicare tax. No Additional Medicare Tax or mandatory Arizona employee payroll tax applies, so the household total is $2,142.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The elderly or disabled household exception removes the SNAP gross-income test but does not establish eligibility; the household must still pass the net-income test after allowable deductions. This household's $56,400 annual income remains too high after the applicable deductions, so it receives no minimum allotment because minimum benefits apply only after eligibility is established.

Age 69 and disability establish potential aged/disabled categorical status, not Medicaid eligibility by themselves. The spouse qualifies through no Arizona Medicaid pathway: the engine assigns medicaid_category NONE, and the spouse’s MAGI income is 2.46 times FPL for MAGI-based categories. The models converted aged/disabled status into eligibility without completing the applicable income and resource tests.

Medicare eligibility applies at age 65, so the 69-year-old spouse qualifies through the age pathway without needing disability-based eligibility or 24 months of SSDI receipt. The spouse’s workers’ compensation and disability facts do not alter that age-based result.

The case turns on two Arizona-specific rules: Arizona subtracts from federal AGI all Social Security benefits included there, and Arizona's standard deduction conforms to the base federal married-filing-jointly amount (about $32,200 for 2026) with no additional age-65 amount. Removing the $4,300 of taxable Social Security leaves $28,000 of wages as Arizona AGI, which is more than $4,000 below the standard deduction, so taxable income is zero and the 2.5% flat tax yields nothing before refundable credits; itemizing is worse at $16,324 of mortgage interest plus real estate taxes. The wrong answers all manufacture a positive base either by shrinking the deduction — inventing $20,000, $22,000, or an unstated ~$22,700 figure, in two cases by grafting a federal-style age-65 add-on Arizona does not have — or by leaving Social Security in the Arizona base. One model produced the zero result and then overrode it, and one returned nothing at all.

Arizona’s refundable credits are not awarded merely because a married filer is elderly and has income below a general threshold. The household satisfies no applicable Arizona refundable-credit eligibility pathway in 2026, so az_refundable_credits and the aggregate state_refundable_credits are both zero; the other failure is a missing required output.

The head is a 79-year-old widow with no dependent child, so she files Single. Taxable Social Security is $16,846: provisional income of $48,525 is run through the single $25k/$34k formula, not the 85% cap. The deductions are the $18,150 standard deduction ($16,100 + $2,050 aged) plus the $6,000 OBBBA senior deduction, so taxable income is $26,430.71. The $4,681 of qualified dividends and capital gains is taxed at 0%, and the $21,749.71 ordinary portion is taxed at 10% up to $12,400 and 12% above, for $2,361.96. The wrong answers fall into two main groups. About a dozen models used qualifying-surviving-spouse status with the joint standard deduction even though that status requires a dependent child, and they came in far too low. About sixteen models dropped the $6,000 senior deduction, either by using TCJA-era amounts without it or by assuming TCJA expired in 2026 and applying personal exemptions and a 15% bracket; they came in too high. A few others mishandled Social Security (taxed it at the 85% cap or left it out), double-counted income, or taxed the 0%-bracket gains at ordinary rates. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned llm_error; adjudicated llm_error (thresholds_rates). The frozen 1,979.16 is regenerated as 2,361.96: it corrects an engine defect fixed upstream (fixed in PolicyEngine/policyengine-us#8839 (issue #8828), after the reference freeze): Capital gain distributions are long-term capital gain in gross income and in the preferential-rate base. Reference regenerated (26 U.S.C. 61(a)(3), 852(b)(3)(B); Form 1040 line 7).
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Payroll tax uses employee wages as its base, and the prompt lists no wage or salary income. The pension, IRA distributions, investment income, Social Security benefits, and farm loss do not generate employee-side Social Security or Medicare tax, so employee payroll tax is $0.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

reference_bug_hypothesis: PolicyEngine's federal AGI drops the $3,753 non-Schedule-D capital gain: AGI less taxable Social Security is $29,981.71, exactly $3,753 below the listed non-SS income of $33,735, and the $13,655.95 taxable-SS figure reproduces to the cent only on that reduced base, which contradicts Form 1040 line 7 and IRC §61(a)(3). Its Wisconsin subtractions also leave out the age-67 retirement-income subtraction of up to $24,000 created by 2025 Wisconsin Act 15, which would cover the $24,086 of IRA and pension income and bring Wisconsin tax to $0.
case_annotation: The reference files the 79-year-old surviving spouse, who has no dependent child, as single. It subtracts only taxable Social Security ($13,655.95) from federal AGI of $43,637.65 to reach WI AGI of $29,981.71, applies the $12,671.36 sliding-scale single deduction and $950 of exemptions, taxes $16,360.34 at 3.5%/4.4% for $584.74, and then subtracts the $300 maximum school property tax credit to get $284.74. Most models answered $0: some subtracted IRA and pension income under the age-67 $24,000 retirement-income subtraction, and others erased the tax with credits that do not exist or with the uncapped school property tax credit. A second group landing at about $420–$480 put the $3,753 non-Schedule-D gain into WI AGI. The higher answers left out the $300 school property tax credit, used married-joint or unreduced standard deductions, applied the old 3.54%/4.65% rates, or kept Social Security in the base. Developer adjudication (2026-09-22): the judge (claude-opus-5-5) returned reference_engine_defect; adjudicated reference_engine_defect (state_local_rule). The frozen reference is 284.74; the corrected value is 0.00. PolicyEngine's Wisconsin tax before refundable credits ignores the retirement income exclusion the filer elects, which its final Wisconsin tax applies; PolicyEngine's Wisconsin capital gain subtraction leaves out capital gain distributions reported without Schedule D, so once they reach federal AGI Wisconsin taxes all of them instead of 70%. Reference is an engine defect; output excluded from scoring (Wis. Stat. 71.05(6)(b)54m (2025 Wisconsin Act 15); 2025 Schedule SB line 16; Wis. Stat. 71.05(6)(b)9; 26 U.S.C. 852(b)(3)(B); 2025 Wisconsin Schedule SB instructions, line 5).

The Wisconsin homestead credit requires qualifying household income and property-tax circumstances to be computed from the stated annual inputs under the 2026 rules. The household receives substantial Social Security, IRA, pension, dividend, interest, and capital-gain income, so reducing household income to roughly $14,420 and applying a maximum-credit shortcut creates a refundable credit that the full eligibility computation does not allow.

The single trap is the upper age limit on the childless EITC: IRC §32(c)(1)(A)(ii)(II) allows the no-qualifying-children credit only to filers at least 25 and under 65 at the close of the tax year, and the American Rescue Plan's one-year suspension of that ceiling applied to 2021 only. The head is 66 in tax year 2026, so the EITC is $0 regardless of the $4,088 in earnings sitting squarely in the phase-in range, and with no children, no education expenses, and no Recovery Rebate or refundable payroll tax credit, total federal refundable credits are $0. All four models jumped straight to the phase-in arithmetic on earned income and never applied the age test, three of them landing on 7.65% × ~$4,088 ≈ $312–313 and one on a fabricated 15.3% rate.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

Low income alone does not place this 66-year-old into a Colorado Medicaid category. The MAGI adult expansion pathway has an age limit, while the aged pathway applies separate categorical and resource rules; with no SSI, no disability status, and $2,800 in bank assets, the engine assigns Medicaid category NONE.
